explanations.B: Reversal: 'only if' makes misrepresentation necessary for deserved criticism, not sufficient, so it cannot establish that the café deserves it.
explanations.C: Opposite: it supports praise, the consideration the critic sets aside.
explanations.D: Wrong force: it says what a business should do when asked; it does not say that failing to do so deserves criticism, and the café's menu made an affirmative claim.
explanations.E: Shell game: it criticizes serving imported produce, but the critic's complaint is the false description, not the sourcing.

keyTakeaway: When a conclusion holds 'nonetheless' despite a conceded merit, the justifying principle must explicitly override that merit.
predictionHint: Misrepresentation deserves criticism no matter how good the food is.

stimulus: City engineer: The Mill Street bridge carries only a fraction of the traffic that the Harbor bridge carries. Even so, the city should repair the Mill Street bridge first, because inspections show that it is far more likely than the Harbor bridge to fail within the next few years.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the city engineer's reasoning?

choices.A: A city should repair the bridges that carry the most traffic before it repairs any of the bridges that carry less traffic.
choices.B: A city should repair any bridge that inspections show is likely to fail within the next few years.
choices.C: If a bridge is the first to be repaired, it must be the bridge that is most likely to fail.
choices.D: A city should immediately close to all traffic any bridge that inspections show is likely to fail within the next few years.
choices.E: In deciding which structures to repair first, a city should give priority by likelihood of failure rather than by amount of use.

explanations.A: Opposite: this principle ranks the Harbor bridge first.
explanations.B: Wrong force: it says the Mill Street bridge should be repaired, but the conclusion is about repairing it 'first,' and the Harbor bridge may also be likely to fail.
explanations.C: Reversal: it states a condition that must hold if a bridge is repaired first, which cannot be used to conclude that the Mill Street bridge should be first.
explanations.D: Shell game: closing a bridge is a different action from repairing it before another bridge.
explanations.E: The engineer weighs likelihood of failure against traffic volume and lets the former win. E states exactly that priority rule, and the facts (higher failure likelihood, lower use) place the Mill Street bridge first under it.

keyTakeaway: A conclusion about ordering ('first') needs a principle about priority, not a principle that merely says the action should be taken.
predictionHint: Rank by risk of failure, not by traffic.

stimulus: Editor: Last week's article misstated the year in which a local judge was first appointed to the bench. Very few readers are likely to have noticed the error, and it had no bearing on the article's main points. We should nonetheless publish a prominent correction, because the error concerned a factual claim about a named individual.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the editor's reasoning?

choices.A: A newspaper should publish a prominent correction only if the error in question concerned a factual claim about a named individual.
choices.B: A newspaper should prominently correct any factual error about a named individual, however few readers noticed it or however minor it was.
choices.C: A newspaper should promptly and prominently correct any error that bears on the main points of the article in which it appeared.
choices.D: A newspaper need not correct an error that very few of its readers are likely to have noticed.
choices.E: A newspaper that publishes an error about a named individual should apologize privately to that individual.

explanations.A: Reversal: 'only if' makes concerning a named individual a requirement for a prominent correction, not a reason to publish one.
explanations.B: The facts are a factual error about a named individual, few readers noticing, and no bearing on the main points. B makes the first fact sufficient and expressly sets aside the other two, which is precisely the editor's reasoning.
explanations.C: Shell game: this error had 'no bearing' on the main points, so the principle's condition is not met.
explanations.D: Opposite: it would excuse the newspaper from correcting this error.
explanations.E: Wrong force: a private apology is a different remedy from a prominent published correction.

keyTakeaway: The justifying principle must track the reason the speaker actually gives and neutralize the considerations the speaker explicitly sets aside.
predictionHint: Errors about named people get corrected prominently, no matter how small.

stimulus: Research director: The laboratory must retract the paper it published last year. The paper's central conclusions are probably still correct, since they have since been confirmed by other research groups. However, it has now come to light that one of the paper's coauthors fabricated a portion of the data on which the paper relied.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the research director's reasoning?

choices.A: A published paper should be retracted only if its central conclusions have been shown to be false.
choices.B: If a published paper is retracted, its authors should be barred from publishing in the same journal in the future.
choices.C: A researcher who is found to have fabricated data should be dismissed from the laboratory that employs the researcher.
choices.D: A paper that relies on fabricated data should be retracted even if its conclusions are likely to be correct.
choices.E: A paper that has been retracted must have relied on data that were fabricated by at least one of its authors.

explanations.A: Opposite: the conclusions are probably correct, so under this principle the paper should not be retracted.
explanations.B: Wrong force: it describes a consequence of retraction, not a ground for it.
explanations.C: Shell game: it prescribes a penalty for the person, not an action regarding the paper.
explanations.D: The premises are fabricated data and probably correct conclusions. D makes the former sufficient for retraction 'even if' the latter holds, which yields the director's conclusion.
explanations.E: Reversal: it states what must be true of a retracted paper, which cannot be used to show that this paper should be retracted.

keyTakeaway: A principle of the form 'retracted papers must have X' never justifies retracting a paper that has X; the direction of the conditional matters.
predictionHint: Fabrication alone requires retraction, correct conclusions or not.

stimulus: Judge: Both parties signed the agreement, and ordinarily a signed term is binding. But the clause waiving the buyer's right to a refund was printed in type so small, and placed so inconspicuously, that no reasonable person reading the agreement would have noticed it. The clause is therefore not enforceable against the buyer.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the judge's reasoning?

choices.A: A term in a signed agreement is enforceable only if a reasonable person reading the agreement would have noticed it.
choices.B: A term in a signed agreement is enforceable if the party against whom it is being enforced actually read the term before signing.
choices.C: A seller should print all terms that limit a buyer's rights in type that is conspicuous and easy to read.
choices.D: A term in a signed agreement is not enforceable against a party who did not understand the term's meaning.
choices.E: A signed agreement is binding on both parties unless one of the parties was coerced into signing it.

explanations.A: The judge's premise is that no reasonable reader would have noticed the clause. A makes being noticeable to a reasonable reader a necessary condition for enforceability, so the premise's failure yields the conclusion that the clause is not enforceable.
explanations.B: Reversal: it gives a condition under which a term is enforceable; it says nothing about when one is not.
explanations.C: Wrong force: it says what sellers should do but does not say what follows for enforceability when they do not.
explanations.D: Shell game: the judge's finding concerns whether a reasonable person would have 'noticed' the clause, not whether the buyer 'understood' it.
explanations.E: Opposite: no coercion occurred, so this principle would make the whole agreement, clause included, binding.

keyTakeaway: To justify a 'not enforceable' conclusion, the principle must state a necessary condition for enforceability that the facts fail.
predictionHint: Unnoticeable to a reasonable reader, therefore not enforceable.

stimulus: Coach: Theo is the most skilled player on the team, but I am naming Rani captain instead. Whenever the team is under pressure, the other players look to Rani for direction, and she settles them. The captain's job is to lead under pressure, and skill at the game is no substitute for that.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the coach's reasoning?

choices.A: A coach should name as captain the player whom the other players on the team most respect.
choices.B: The most skilled player on a team should never be named captain of that team.
choices.C: A coach should name a player captain only if that player has demonstrated the ability to lead teammates when the team is under pressure.
choices.D: A coach should consult the players on the team before deciding whom to name captain.
choices.E: In choosing a captain, a coach should weigh ability to lead teammates under pressure more heavily than skill at the game.

explanations.A: Shell game: the coach's evidence is that players 'look to Rani for direction,' not that they most respect her; respect is a different quality.
explanations.B: Extreme: it would rule out Theo but gives no reason to choose Rani, and it is far broader than anything the coach says.
explanations.C: Necessary versus sufficient: 'only if' sets a requirement Rani meets, but it does not say that leadership outweighs skill, so it cannot justify choosing Rani over Theo.
explanations.D: Wrong force: consulting the players is a procedure, not a basis for the choice the coach made.
explanations.E: The coach faces a trade-off between Theo's skill and Rani's leadership under pressure and chooses leadership. E states that priority, and the facts place Rani ahead under it.

keyTakeaway: When a conclusion picks one option over another on competing criteria, the principle must rank the criteria, not just impose a threshold.
predictionHint: Leadership under pressure outweighs skill.

stimulus: Historian: The general's memoir states that the retreat was ordered before the river crossing, whereas the official campaign record places the order afterward. On this point we should trust the memoir. The general, writing privately decades later, had nothing to gain from misstating the sequence, while the officers who compiled the record were anxious to deflect blame for the crossing's heavy losses.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.A: If one account of an event should be preferred over a conflicting account, its author must have had no motive whatever to misrepresent the event.
choices.B: An account of an event written by a participant in the event is more reliable than an account compiled by others afterward.
choices.C: When two accounts conflict, the account whose author had no motive to misrepresent the event should be preferred over one whose author did.
choices.D: Historians should take into account the motives of an author when assessing the reliability of that author's account.
choices.E: If the author of an account had a motive to misrepresent an event, that account should be disregarded entirely.

explanations.A: Reversal: it states a condition that must hold if an account is preferred; it does not say that meeting the condition makes an account preferable.
explanations.B: Shell game: the officers who compiled the record were also participants, and the historian's reasoning turns on motive, not participation.
explanations.C: The premises are a conflict between two accounts, no motive on the general's side, and a motive on the officers' side. C converts exactly those facts into the conclusion that the memoir should be preferred.
explanations.D: Wrong force: 'take into account' calls for a consideration; it does not say which account to trust.
explanations.E: Half right: it would discard the official record, but discarding one account does not by itself establish that the other should be trusted.

keyTakeaway: A comparative conclusion ('trust X over Y') needs a comparative principle that uses the contrast the argument draws.
predictionHint: Prefer the account from the writer with no reason to lie.

stimulus: Physician: Mr. Osei's adult children have asked me to tell them his diagnosis. They are plainly worried about him and want to help. But Mr. Osei, who fully understands his condition and its implications, has asked me not to discuss it with anyone, so I will not tell them.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the physician's reasoning?

choices.A: A physician should disclose a patient's diagnosis to family members who are in a position to help the patient.
choices.B: A physician may disclose the diagnosis of a patient who understands his or her condition only with that patient's consent.
choices.C: A physician may withhold a patient's diagnosis from family members if the patient is unable to understand the condition or its implications.
choices.D: A physician must disclose a patient's diagnosis to anyone the patient designates to receive it.
choices.E: A physician should weigh a patient's request for confidentiality against the concerns of the patient's family.

explanations.A: Opposite: the children want to help, so this principle would require disclosure.
explanations.B: The facts are a patient who 'fully understands his condition' and has refused consent. B makes consent necessary for disclosure in exactly that case, so the refusal yields the physician's conclusion.
explanations.C: Shell game: its condition is a patient 'unable to understand,' but Mr. Osei fully understands, so the principle does not apply.
explanations.D: Reversal: it says what the physician must do when the patient designates someone; it is silent about what to do when the patient refuses.
explanations.E: Wrong force: weighing the two considerations does not determine that confidentiality wins.

keyTakeaway: Check that the principle's antecedent matches the facts stated, especially a qualifier like 'understands' that the stimulus goes out of its way to include.
predictionHint: No consent from a competent patient, no disclosure.

stimulus: Planning commissioner: The proposed development includes more green space than our regulations require, yet the commission should reject it. Nearly all of the green space lies on a steep slope behind a retaining wall, where no resident could use it. The purpose of the green-space requirement is to give residents places to walk and gather, and this proposal does not serve that purpose.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the planning commissioner's reasoning?

choices.A: A proposal that provides more than the required amount of green space should be approved if that green space is usable by the development's residents.
choices.B: The commission should amend its regulations to require that green space be located on level ground.
choices.C: A development proposal should be approved only if it includes at least the amount of green space that the regulations require.
choices.D: A proposal should be rejected if it satisfies the letter of a requirement without serving the purpose for which the requirement was adopted.
choices.E: Regulations should be rewritten whenever developers find ways to satisfy them without serving their underlying purpose.

explanations.A: Reversal: it gives a sufficient condition for approval, and its condition is unmet here anyway, so it yields nothing about rejection.
explanations.B: Wrong force: amending the regulations is a different action from rejecting this proposal under the current ones.
explanations.C: Necessary versus sufficient: the proposal meets this requirement, so the principle gives no ground to reject it.
explanations.D: The premises are that the proposal meets the quantity requirement (the letter) but provides no usable space (fails the purpose). D makes that combination sufficient for rejection, which is the conclusion.
explanations.E: Shell game: it concerns what to do about the regulations, not what to do about this proposal.

keyTakeaway: When a speaker rejects something that meets a stated rule, the justifying principle must elevate the rule's purpose over its letter.
predictionHint: Meeting the rule's letter but not its purpose is grounds for rejection.

stimulus: Economist: Critics fault the central bank for raising interest rates last spring, since inflation fell sharply over the following months for reasons unrelated to the increase, and the higher rates slowed growth. But the bank's decision was the right one. Every reliable indicator available in the spring pointed to accelerating inflation, and raising rates is the appropriate response to such indicators.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.A: Whether a policy decision was right depends on the evidence available when it was made, not on what later occurred.
choices.B: A central bank should raise interest rates only when reliable indicators point to accelerating inflation.
choices.C: A policy decision that produces worse outcomes than the alternative would have cannot be considered the right decision.
choices.D: A central bank that has correctly read the available indicators should not be blamed if its policies slow growth.
choices.E: If a policy decision was the right one, then it was based on the best evidence available at the time it was made.

explanations.A: The critics judge by outcomes; the economist judges by the evidence in the spring. A makes the economist's standard the correct one and excludes the critics' ('not on what later occurred'), so the facts about the indicators yield 'the decision was the right one.'
explanations.B: Necessary versus sufficient: 'only when' permits raising rates in these conditions but does not make doing so right.
explanations.C: Opposite: it adopts the critics' outcome-based standard and would condemn the decision.
explanations.D: Shell game: 'should not be blamed' is weaker than 'was the right one,' and D excuses only the slowing of growth, not the decision as a whole given that inflation fell anyway.
explanations.E: Reversal: it states what must be true of a right decision; it cannot be used to show that this decision was right.

keyTakeaway: When a speaker defends a decision against hindsight, the principle must fix the standard of evaluation, not merely excuse one consequence.
predictionHint: Judge the decision by what was known then, not by what happened later.

stimulus: Ethicist: When Marguerite told her colleague that the quarterly report had been finished, the report was in fact still incomplete. Yet Marguerite was not being dishonest. Her assistant had told her that morning that the report was done, and she had no reason to doubt him.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.A: A person who relies on an assistant's word is not responsible for any errors that the assistant makes.
choices.B: If a person believes a statement to be false when making it, then the person is being dishonest in making it.
choices.C: A person should verify any information received from a subordinate before repeating it to others as fact.
choices.D: A person who makes a statement that is in fact true is not being dishonest, whatever the person believes about it.
choices.E: A person who makes a false statement is being dishonest only if the person believes the statement to be false.

explanations.A: Shell game: not being 'responsible for errors' is a different matter from not being dishonest.
explanations.B: Reversal: it says believing a statement false makes one dishonest; it does not say that lacking that belief makes one honest, which is what the ethicist needs.
explanations.C: Wrong force: it says what Marguerite should have done, which if anything counts against her rather than clearing her of dishonesty.
explanations.D: Shell game: its antecedent is a statement that is 'in fact true,' but Marguerite's statement was false, so the principle does not apply.
explanations.E: Marguerite's statement was false, but she believed it true on her assistant's word. E makes believing the statement false a necessary condition of dishonesty; since that condition fails, she was not dishonest.

keyTakeaway: To justify 'not X,' find the principle that makes a missing fact necessary for X; a principle giving a sufficient condition for X cannot do it.
predictionHint: Dishonesty requires believing you are saying something false.

stimulus: A customer asked a mechanic to disconnect the warning system that alerts a driver when the car's brakes are failing, because the customer found its frequent alerts annoying. The mechanic refused, even though the customer insisted and offered to pay extra for the work. The mechanic acted correctly.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: A service provider should perform any lawful service that a customer requests and is willing to pay for.
choices.B: A service provider should explain to a customer why a requested service is inadvisable before performing it.
choices.C: A service provider may refuse to perform a requested service if the provider finds the customer's request or manner annoying.
choices.D: A service provider should refuse a requested service if performing it would create a serious risk to the safety of others.
choices.E: If a service provider refuses a customer's request, the provider must have had concerns about safety.

explanations.A: Opposite: it would require the mechanic to do the work.
explanations.B: Wrong force: it calls for an explanation before performing the service, not for refusing it.
explanations.C: Shell game: it was the customer who found the alerts annoying, and annoyance is not the basis on which the mechanic refused.
explanations.D: Disabling a brake-failure warning creates a serious safety risk to the driver and others on the road. D makes refusing such a request the correct course, which justifies the judgment that the mechanic acted correctly.
explanations.E: Reversal: it describes what must be true when a provider refuses; it cannot be used to show that refusing was correct.

keyTakeaway: A conform principle must make the action taken the right one given the stated facts; a principle about what must be true after the fact does not.
predictionHint: Refuse work that endangers people, whatever the customer wants.

stimulus: Jurist: The witness's account was obtained after the police threatened to charge her brother unless she cooperated. Her account is probably accurate, since it matches physical evidence found at the scene. Nevertheless, the court should have excluded it from the trial.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: Testimony should be excluded from a trial only if it was obtained by means of threats against the witness.
choices.B: Testimony obtained by means of threats should be excluded from trial regardless of whether the testimony is accurate.
choices.C: Testimony that is corroborated by physical evidence found at the scene should be admitted at trial.
choices.D: Courts should take into account the circumstances under which testimony was obtained when deciding how much weight to give it.
choices.E: Testimony obtained by means of threats is unlikely to be accurate and should therefore be regarded with suspicion.

explanations.A: Reversal: 'only if' makes threats a necessary condition for exclusion, not a reason to exclude.
explanations.B: The facts are testimony obtained by threats and probable accuracy. B makes threats sufficient for exclusion 'regardless of' accuracy, which is exactly the jurist's 'nevertheless.'
explanations.C: Opposite: the account is corroborated, so this principle would admit it.
explanations.D: Wrong force: adjusting the 'weight' given to testimony is not excluding it.
explanations.E: Shell game: it rests exclusion on inaccuracy, but the jurist concedes the account is probably accurate, and 'suspicion' is not exclusion.

keyTakeaway: When the speaker concedes a point that cuts the other way, the principle must explicitly override that point.
predictionHint: Coerced testimony is out, accurate or not.

stimulus: The Wexford Museum purchased a carved panel at a public auction thirty years ago, and the purchase was entirely lawful. It has recently been established that the panel had been smuggled out of its country of origin in violation of that country's laws decades before the auction. The museum has decided to return the panel, and it is right to do so.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: An institution that acquires an object lawfully is entitled to retain it regardless of the object's earlier history.
choices.B: An institution should return an object to its country of origin only if the institution's own acquisition of that object was itself unlawful.
choices.C: An institution should return an object that was unlawfully removed from its country of origin, even if it acquired the object lawfully.
choices.D: An institution should thoroughly investigate the history of an object before it purchases the object.
choices.E: An institution that returns an object to its country of origin should be compensated for the price it originally paid.

explanations.A: Opposite: it would entitle the museum to keep the panel.
explanations.B: Reversal: 'only if' sets a necessary condition for return that the museum's lawful purchase fails, so it would count against returning the panel.
explanations.C: The facts are unlawful removal from the country of origin and a lawful later purchase. C makes the first sufficient for return 'even if' the second holds, which yields the judgment that returning the panel is right.
explanations.D: Wrong force: a duty to investigate before buying says nothing about what to do with an object already owned.
explanations.E: Shell game: compensation is a separate question from whether return is the right course.

keyTakeaway: Look for the principle whose 'even if' clause neutralizes the fact that seems to point the other way.
predictionHint: Unlawfully removed objects go back, lawful purchase notwithstanding.

stimulus: A software company discovered a flaw in its product that could allow intruders to gain access to customers' data. No fix was yet available, and announcing the flaw would alert potential intruders to it. The company announced it immediately anyway, so that customers could disconnect affected systems until a fix was ready. The company acted properly.
stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.A: People exposed to a risk should be told of it whenever knowing enables them to protect themselves, even if disclosure increases the risk for some.
choices.B: A company should disclose a flaw in one of its products only after a fix for that flaw has become available to customers.
choices.C: A company that discovers a flaw in one of its products should develop and distribute a fix for the flaw as quickly as possible.
choices.D: A company is not responsible for harm resulting from a flaw in its product if it has told its customers how to avoid that harm.
choices.E: If a company acted properly in disclosing a product flaw, then its customers were able to protect themselves as a result of that disclosure.

explanations.A: The facts are that disclosure let customers 'disconnect affected systems' (protect themselves) but also alerted intruders (increased risk for some). A makes the first consideration decisive 'even if' the second holds, so announcing immediately was proper.
explanations.B: Opposite: no fix was available, so this principle would condemn the announcement.
explanations.C: Wrong force: a duty to fix quickly says nothing about whether to disclose before the fix exists.
explanations.D: Shell game: not being 'responsible for harm' is a different judgment from having 'acted properly,' and D concerns liability after harm rather than the decision to disclose.
explanations.E: Reversal: it states a consequence of having acted properly and so cannot establish that the company did.

keyTakeaway: When a decision trades one risk against another, the justifying principle must say which consideration wins, and the facts must fall on the winning side.
predictionHint: Warn people when warning lets them protect themselves, even at some cost.

stimulus: Principle: A landlord may enter a tenant's apartment without giving notice only in an emergency that threatens the safety of persons or serious damage to property; in all other cases, the landlord must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice before entering.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: A landlord entered an apartment without notice to repair a dripping faucet that the tenant had reported a week earlier.
choices.B: A landlord entered an apartment without notice after seeing water pouring from beneath its door into the hallway and stairwell below.
choices.C: A landlord gave a tenant 12 hours' notice before entering to conduct a routine annual inspection, reasoning that the tenant would be at home anyway.
choices.D: A landlord entered an apartment without notice to show it to a prospective tenant who was able to visit only that afternoon.
choices.E: A landlord entered an apartment without notice to retrieve a tool he had left behind during a repair the previous day.

explanations.A: Shell game: a repair is a legitimate reason to enter, but a faucet reported 'a week earlier' is not an emergency, so notice was required.
explanations.B: Water 'pouring' into the hallway and stairwell threatens serious damage to property, which is the one condition under which entry without notice is permitted. The landlord's action fits the principle exactly.
explanations.C: Half right: notice was given, but '12 hours' falls short of the required 24, and the tenant's presence is not an exception the principle recognizes.
explanations.D: Shell game: the prospective tenant's schedule creates urgency, but urgency is not an 'emergency that threatens the safety of persons or serious damage to property.'
explanations.E: Opposite: retrieving a forgotten tool is a nonemergency entry without any notice, the plainest violation of the principle.

keyTakeaway: An exception stated with 'only in' is narrow; a case must match its exact terms, not merely be pressing or convenient.
predictionHint: No notice is fine only for a genuine emergency.

stimulus: Principle: A scholarly journal should publish a critique of an article that it previously published only if the critique's author has first given the article's author an opportunity to respond to the critique, and any response that is made must be published alongside the critique.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: A journal published a critique together with a response that the journal's editors had solicited from the article's author after accepting the critique.
choices.B: A journal published a critique its author had sent to the article's author in advance; that author declined to respond, so the critique appeared alone.
choices.C: A journal published a critique whose author had first given the article's author an opportunity to respond, then printed that response in the following issue.
choices.D: A journal published a critique without contacting the article's author because the critique concerned only a minor point of methodology.
choices.E: A journal published a critique alongside a response written by a colleague of the article's author, whom the critique's author had contacted instead.

explanations.A: Half right: a response appeared alongside the critique, but the opportunity to respond must come from 'the critique's author' and must come 'first,' not from the editors after acceptance.
explanations.B: The critique's author gave the article's author an advance opportunity to respond, satisfying the first condition. The second condition governs 'any response'; since none was made, publishing the critique alone violates nothing.
explanations.C: Half right: the opportunity was given, but the response was printed 'in the following issue' rather than 'alongside the critique.'
explanations.D: Out of scope: the principle contains no exception for minor points, so skipping the opportunity to respond violates it.
explanations.E: Shell game: the opportunity must go to 'the article's author,' not to a colleague.

keyTakeaway: A condition on 'any response' is satisfied vacuously when there is no response; do not read it as requiring one.
predictionHint: Offered a chance to respond, and published whatever response came alongside.

stimulus: Principle: A physician may override a patient's stated treatment preference only when the patient lacks the capacity to understand the consequences of that preference, and even in such a case the physician may override the preference only to the extent necessary to prevent serious harm to the patient.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: A physician administered a transfusion to a patient who had refused one after calmly explaining that she understood she might die without it.
choices.B: A physician, finding a delirious patient refusing all treatment, gave antibiotics for a life-threatening infection and also performed a nonurgent procedure the patient had declined.
choices.C: A physician, finding a delirious patient refusing all treatment, administered fluids for severe dehydration but postponed an elective procedure the patient had earlier declined.
choices.D: A physician sedated an agitated but lucid patient who kept refusing a routine blood test, reasoning that the refusal was irrational.
choices.E: A physician overrode a confused patient's refusal of a bandage change to spare the patient minor discomfort, since the patient could not understand its purpose.

explanations.A: Opposite: the patient understood the consequences, so the first condition fails and the override is forbidden.
explanations.B: Half right: the patient lacked capacity, and the antibiotics were necessary, but the 'nonurgent procedure' exceeds 'the extent necessary to prevent serious harm.'
explanations.C: The patient is delirious (lacks capacity), fluids for 'severe dehydration' prevent serious harm, and the physician stopped there by postponing the elective procedure. Both conditions are met and the limit is respected.
explanations.D: Shell game: 'irrational' is not the same as lacking 'the capacity to understand the consequences,' and the patient is described as lucid; a routine test also does not involve serious harm.
explanations.E: Half right: the capacity condition is met, but 'minor discomfort' is not 'serious harm,' so the override exceeds what the principle permits.

keyTakeaway: A two-part rule with 'and even then only' requires the case to satisfy the trigger and respect the limit; the best trap satisfies one and not the other.
predictionHint: Incapacitated patient, serious harm prevented, nothing extra done.

stimulus: Principle: A public official should recuse himself or herself from any decision from which the official or a member of the official's immediate family stands to gain financially. A merely speculative future gain does not require recusal, but an official who is uncertain whether a potential gain is speculative should obtain an ethics ruling before participating.
stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.A: An official whose spouse owns shares in a company bidding on a contract helped award it, since the shares were few and the gain trivial.
choices.B: An official unsure whether a zoning decision would affect her brother's property value voted on it anyway, reasoning that any effect was probably speculative.
choices.C: An official who stood to gain personally from a licensing decision obtained an ethics ruling and participated after the ruling approved his doing so.
choices.D: An official who could not determine whether his sister's consulting firm would benefit from a proposed regulation requested an ethics ruling before taking part.
choices.E: An official voted on a stadium subsidy although his daughter's company held the concessions contract there, because the contract predated his election.

explanations.A: Shell game: a 'small' gain is still a definite gain to immediate family, not a 'speculative' one, so recusal was required.
explanations.B: Half right: the official correctly recognized uncertainty, but the principle requires an ethics ruling in that case, not the official's own guess that the gain was 'probably speculative.'
explanations.C: Half right: the ethics-ruling procedure applies only to uncertain cases; an official who definitely stands to gain 'should recuse,' and a ruling does not substitute for that.
explanations.D: The official is uncertain whether a potential gain to immediate family (his sister) is speculative, which is exactly the situation in which the principle directs obtaining an ethics ruling before participating.
explanations.E: Out of scope: when the contract was signed is irrelevant to the principle; the daughter's definite financial stake required recusal.

keyTakeaway: Match the case to the right branch of a multi-branch rule: a definite gain, a speculative gain, and an uncertain gain each call for a different action.
predictionHint: Uncertain about the gain, so get the ruling first.

stimulus: Marketing director: Our company's sales rose 15 percent in the six months after we launched our new advertising campaign. The campaign was expensive, but these results show that it was worth the cost, since it clearly brought in substantial new business.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the sales of competing companies that ran no new advertising rose by a comparable amount over the same six months
choices.B: Whether the company's sales did in fact rise by a full 15 percent during the six months after the campaign was launched
choices.C: Whether the company plans to continue running the advertising campaign for an additional six months
choices.D: Whether the 15 percent increase was the largest six-month increase in sales in the company's entire history
choices.E: Whether customers who made purchases during the six months found the campaign's advertisements entertaining

explanations.A: The argument attributes the rise to the campaign. If competitors without new advertising rose comparably, the increase was probably market-wide and the campaign gets no credit; if they did not, the campaign is the likely cause. The two answers push in opposite directions.
explanations.B: Premise booster: confirming the premise does not test the inference from the sales rise to the campaign's effect.
explanations.C: Out of scope: future plans do not bear on whether the past campaign caused the increase.
explanations.D: Wrong force: how the increase ranks historically says nothing about what caused it.
explanations.E: Shell game: whether customers were entertained is a reaction to the advertisements, not evidence about whether they drove purchases.

keyTakeaway: For a before-and-after causal claim, the most useful question asks what happened to a comparable group that did not get the treatment.
predictionHint: Did everyone's sales go up?

stimulus: Historian: Tax rolls from the town of Brevik show that the number of new houses built each decade fell steadily during the century before the plague arrived. Since people build new houses when new households are being formed, Brevik's population must have been declining well before the plague.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the plague caused a greater decline in Brevik's population than in the populations of neighboring towns
choices.B: Whether the tax rolls of Brevik from the century before the plague have survived intact
choices.C: Whether, during that century, Brevik's authorities restricted new construction within the town walls
choices.D: Whether the houses built in Brevik during that century were constructed primarily for wealthy residents
choices.E: Whether most of the new houses in Brevik were built by couples who had recently married

explanations.A: Out of scope: what the plague did afterward does not bear on the population trend before it.
explanations.B: Wrong force: even perfectly preserved rolls leave open whether fewer houses means fewer households, which is the inference at issue.
explanations.C: The argument reads fewer new houses as fewer new households. If construction was restricted, the decline in building reflects regulation rather than population and the argument collapses; if it was not, the inference stands. The answers cut opposite ways.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the wealth of those who built does not affect whether declining construction tracks declining population.
explanations.E: Premise booster: it elaborates the premise that house building accompanies household formation but does not test whether the decline in building had another cause.

keyTakeaway: When an argument uses one quantity as a proxy for another, the most useful question asks whether something else could have moved the proxy.
predictionHint: Was there some other reason people stopped building?

stimulus: Conservationist: Five years ago, the collection of the rare Vellman orchid from the wild was banned. Yet the number of Vellman orchids sold each year in the country's flower markets is as high as it was before the ban. The ban, therefore, has failed to protect wild populations of the orchid.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether the penalties for violating the ban on collecting the Vellman orchid are severe enough to deter most would-be collectors
choices.B: Whether the ban on collecting the Vellman orchid was supported by most of the country's botanists
choices.C: How many people are employed in selling orchids in the country's flower markets
choices.D: Whether the Vellman orchid is more difficult to cultivate than other orchids sold in the markets
choices.E: Whether the Vellman orchids now sold in flower markets are grown from cultivated stock rather than collected from the wild

explanations.A: Wrong force: deterrence bears only indirectly on what is happening; strong penalties could still be evaded, and weak penalties could still go unexploited, so neither answer settles where the orchids come from.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: expert support for the ban does not tell us whether it has worked.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the size of the orchid trade workforce has no bearing on the origin of the orchids sold.
explanations.D: Shell game: difficulty of cultivation hints at origin but does not establish it; difficult plants can still be cultivated commercially.
explanations.E: The argument equates steady market sales with continued wild collection. If the orchids sold are cultivated, sales can stay high while wild populations are protected, and the argument fails; if they are wild-collected, the argument is strongly supported.

keyTakeaway: When an argument treats a market statistic as a proxy for an illegal activity, ask whether the market could be supplied another way.
predictionHint: Where are the orchids in the markets coming from?

stimulus: Columnist: Since the law requiring chain restaurants to post calorie counts on their menus took effect, the average number of calories in orders placed at those restaurants has fallen by 5 percent. Clearly the posted counts have led diners to choose lower-calorie meals than they otherwise would have chosen.
stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the argument?

choices.A: Whether most diners at chain restaurants are aware that the posting of calorie counts is required by law
choices.B: Whether chain restaurants reformulated or replaced their highest-calorie menu items after the law took effect
choices.C: Whether the calorie counts posted by chain restaurants are accurate within a reasonable margin of error
choices.D: Whether diners who saw the posted calorie counts report that the counts influenced their choices
choices.E: Whether diners at chain restaurants tend to be more health-conscious than diners at independent restaurants not covered by the law

explanations.A: Out of scope: why the counts are posted has no bearing on whether they changed choices.
explanations.B: The conclusion is that diners chose differently. If restaurants cut calories from the items themselves, the average per order can fall 5 percent with diners choosing exactly as before, which undermines the argument; if menus were unchanged, the drop must reflect different choices, which supports it.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant: diners respond to the numbers they see, so the inference about their choices does not depend on whether those numbers are accurate.
explanations.D: Wrong force: self-reports about influence are weak evidence either way, and even diners who credit the counts could have ordered the same items if the items simply had fewer calories, so this question does not settle the alternative explanation.
explanations.E: Shell game: a standing difference between diner populations cannot explain a change over time at chain restaurants.

keyTakeaway: When a conclusion attributes an average change to people's choices, ask whether the options themselves changed.
predictionHint: Did the food change, or did the choices?
